text: Paradoxically the standard model of rational choice. <break time="0.8s" /> By assuming that people always make the single best decision. <break time="0.8s" /> Actually strips away our agency. <break time="0.8s" /> And limits freedom of choice. <break time="0.8s" /> In this way of thinking. <break time="0.8s" /> The perfectly rational Homo economicus. <break time="0.8s" /> Does not really have any options. <break time="0.8s" /> They are expected. <break time="0.8s" /> To always pick just the very best one. <break time="0.8s" /> If they do anything different. <break time="0.8s" /> Their actions are either ignored. <break time="0.8s" /> Or simply called irrational. <break time="0.8s" /> The rational economic actor is paradoxically constrained. <break time="0.8s" /> By the models limited definition. <break time="0.8s" /> Of what counts as good behavior. <break time="0.8s" /> By insisting on a single, rigid standard of rationality. <break time="0.8s" /> The mainstream model ironically denies. <break time="0.8s" /> The very thing it claims to uphold. <break time="0.8s" /> The human capacity for reason and self determination. <break time="0.8s" /> In this sense. <break time="0.8s" /> The rational choice model is not just descriptively inaccurate. <break time="0.8s" /> But also prescriptively dangerous. <break time="0.8s" /> By holding up Homo economicus. <break time="0.8s" /> As the standard to which all behavior should converge. <break time="0.8s" /> It creates a kind of economic peer pressure. <break time="0.8s" /> That stigmatizes and punishes anyone. <break time="0.8s" /> Who does not fit the mold. <break time="0.8s" /> It says, in effect. <break time="0.8s" /> You are not rational enough. <break time="0.8s" /> So you are not good enough.
